title: Cap. VI Arg. 4: from the difference of divine vocation — Jesuits and Arminians forced to grant it
latin: Quarto, disputamus a discrimine vocationis Divinae, quam ipsi Jesuitas atque Arminiani coguntur agnoscere. Sic autem instituitur haec ratio nostra: Si Deus quosdam vocat peculiari quadam vocatione (quam Apostolus, Rom. viii. 28, vocat vocationem secundum propositum; quam Prosper specialem vocationem, De vocat. Gent. 2. 23; Augustinus, vocationem qua fit credens, De Praed. Sanct. cap. 16, et vocationem secundum propositum, qua Deus implet quod praedestinavit, ibid. cap. 17, et gratiam occultam quae a nullo duro corde respuitur, ibid. cap. 8; quam denique ipsi Jesuitae vocationem congruentem et altam indigitant) — si inquam sit talis omnium electorum et non nisi electorum vocatio, tum clarum est Deum eosdem praedestinasse voluntate praevisam illorum fidem antecedente.
pass_a: Fourthly, we dispute from the difference of Divine vocation, which the Jesuits themselves and the Arminians are compelled to acknowledge. And so this our reason is instituted: If God calls certain ones with a certain peculiar vocation (which the Apostle, Rom. 8:28, calls vocation according to purpose; which Prosper calls special vocation, On the Calling of the Gentiles 2.23; Augustine, the vocation by which one becomes a believer, On the Predestination of the Saints ch. 16, and vocation according to purpose, by which God fulfills what he predestined, ibid. ch. 17, and hidden grace which is refused by no hard heart, ibid. ch. 8; which finally the Jesuits themselves point out as congruent and high vocation) — if, I say, there is such a vocation of all the elect and of the elect only, then it is clear that God predestined the same with a will antecedent to their foresighted faith.
pass_b: Fourth argument: from the difference of divine calling — which even Jesuits and Arminians must grant. If God calls some with a peculiar vocation (Paul's vocation according to purpose, Rom. 8:28; Prosper's special vocation; Augustine's vocation that makes a believer, and vocation according to purpose by which God fulfills what he predestined, and hidden grace no hard heart refuses; the Jesuits' congruent and high vocation) — if that calling is of all the elect and of none but the elect, then God clearly predestined them with a will that goes before any foresight of their faith.

title: Cap. VI Arg. 4: media answer the end — efficacious means given elect before foresight of faith
latin: Mediorum enim administratio respondet intentioni finis per eadem media obtinendi. Deus in hac vocatione electis, ac solis electis, administrat media quae novit fore infallibiliter efficacia, atque eo animo administrat, ut sint infallibiliter efficacia, idque ante omnem praevisionem fidei et conversionis in iisdem. Talia media preparari quibusdam ex mero Dei beneplacito, et non ex praevisa eorum fide, clarum est; quia infallibilis productio fidei et paenitentiae ex tali vocatione, tanquam effectus ex causa, consequitur. Si enim talia media hominibus quantumvis obduratis fuissent praeparata ac taliter administrata, illi etiam credidissent ac conversi fuissent.
pass_a: For the administration of means answers to the intention of the end to be obtained through the same means. God in this vocation administers to the elect, and to the elect alone, means which he knows will be infallibly efficacious, and administers them with that mind, that they may be infallibly efficacious, and that before every foresight of faith and conversion in the same. That such means are prepared for certain ones from the mere good pleasure of God, and not from their foresighted faith, is clear; because the infallible production of faith and penitence from such vocation follows as effect from cause. For if such means had been prepared and so administered to men however hardened, they also would have believed and been converted.
pass_b: Means answer the end they are meant to secure. In this vocation God gives the elect — and only the elect — means he knows will be infallibly efficacious, and gives them so that they will be, and that before any foresight of their faith or conversion. That such means are prepared for some from mere good pleasure, not foresighted faith, is plain: faith and penitence follow from such calling as effect from cause. Had the same means been so prepared and given even to the most hardened, they too would have believed and turned.

lemmas.gloss: administration of means answers the end

title: Cap. VI Arg. 4: Augustine John 6:45 — special vocation implies antecedent will to save
latin: Sic Augustinus de praedestinatis et praeteritis disputans ex illo loco, Omnis qui audivit a Patre, et didicit, venit ad me, Joann. vi. 45: Hos omnes, inquit, docet venire ad Christum Deus, hos omnes vult salvos fieri, et in agnitionem veritatis venire. Nam si illos etiam, quibus stultitia est verbum Crucis, ut ad Christum venirent, docere voluisset, proculdubio venirent et ipsi. In hac igitur speciali vocatione agnoscamus necesse est specialem et antecedentem voluntatem salvandi sic vocatos.
pass_a: So Augustine, disputing of the predestined and the passed-by from that place, Everyone who has heard from the Father, and has learned, comes to me, John 6:45: All these, he says, God teaches to come to Christ, all these he wills to be saved, and to come to the knowledge of the truth. For if he had also willed to teach those for whom the word of the Cross is foolishness, that they might come to Christ, without doubt they also would have come. In this special vocation therefore we must necessarily acknowledge a special and antecedent will of saving those so called.
pass_b: So Augustine on the predestined and the passed-by, from John 6:45 (Everyone who has heard from the Father and learned comes to me): all these God teaches to come to Christ; all these he wills saved and brought to the knowledge of the truth. Had he also willed to teach those for whom the Cross is foolishness to come to Christ, they too would have come. In this special vocation, then, we must grant a special antecedent will to save those so called.

lemmas.gloss: all who learn from the Father come
antecedent will of saving the called

title: Cap. VI Arg. 4: Augustine, Arminius, Vorstius — unequal conversion; absolute mercy
latin: De qua idem Augustinus: Deo volenti salvum facere nullum humanum resistit arbitrium; Deo volenti salvum facere sub conditione, Si homines velint credere, resistit arbitrium plurimorum: vult itaque quosdam salvos facere absoluto beneplacito praecurrente et causante eorum fidem, non praerequirente. Hujus rei consideratio eo adegit Arminium, ut fateretur, Deum non aequaliter omnium conversionem et salutem operari. At qui prudenter operatur, ex intentione finis dirigit ac gubernat modum suae operationis. Fuit ergo specialis voluntas et intentio salvandi quosdam ante eorum fidem praevisam, unde nascebatur illa specialis Dei vocatio et operatio, quae fidem in illorum cordibus gignebat. Quinetiam Vorstius, considerata hac speciali quorundam vocatione, concedit nobis exerceri erga quosdam extraordinariam quandam misericordiam, quae ab omni promissione libera et absoluta est: atque hujus respectu illud dici, Miserebitur quorum vult, Apud Piscat. in Resp. Apolog. pag. 17.
pass_a: Of which the same Augustine: To God willing to make safe no human choice resists; to God willing to make safe under the condition, If men will to believe, the choice of very many resists: he therefore wills to make certain ones safe by absolute good pleasure preceding and causing their faith, not presupposing it. Consideration of this matter drove Arminius to the point of confessing that God does not work the conversion and salvation of all equally. But he who operates prudently directs and governs the mode of his operation from the intention of the end. There was therefore a special will and intention of saving certain ones before their foresighted faith, whence was born that special vocation and operation of God which begot faith in their hearts. Moreover Vorstius, having considered this special vocation of certain ones, concedes to us that toward certain ones there is exercised a certain extraordinary mercy, which is free from every promise and absolute: and in respect of this that is said, He will have mercy on whom he will, in Piscator, Reply to the Apology, p. 17.
pass_b: Augustine again: when God wills to save outright, no human will resists; when he wills to save only if men will believe, most wills resist — so he wills to save some by absolute good pleasure that goes before and causes their faith, not that presupposes it. That thought drove Arminius to admit God does not work everyone's conversion and salvation equally. But a prudent agent shapes his work from the end he intends. So there was a special will to save some before foresight of their faith — and from it sprang that special calling and working that begot faith in their hearts. Vorstius, weighing the same special vocation, grants that toward some God exercises an extraordinary mercy free of every promise and absolute — and in that sense, He will have mercy on whom he will (Piscator, Reply to the Apology, p. 17).

lemmas.gloss: he will have mercy on whom he will

title: Cap. VI Arg. 4 close: special vocation of mercy — election ad fidem, not ex fide
latin: In summam redigo hanc rationem. Est quaedam vocatio specialis misericordiae, quae administratur hominibus quibusdam, non quia fuerunt considerati ut fideles, sed quia praedestinati ut fierent fideles. Haec vocatio fluxit ab antecedanea voluntate tales ad vitam aeternam infallibiliter destinante. Non omnium talis est vocatio, sed tantum electorum. Ergo electio ex beneplacito Dei non ex actu hominum dependet. Ergo est ad fidem, non ex fide. Nam hac vocatione voluntas cujusliber praedestinati, ut credat efficaciter, excitatur, etiam si tam sit aversus et ferox ut credentes persequatur, August. Contra 2. Epist. Pelag. lib. 1. cap. 19.
pass_a: I reduce this reason into a sum. There is a certain special vocation of mercy, which is administered to certain men, not because they were considered as faithful, but because they were predestined that they might become faithful. This vocation flowed from an antecedent will infallibly destining such ones to eternal life. Not of all is such a vocation, but only of the elect. Therefore election depends from the good pleasure of God, not from the act of men. Therefore it is unto faith, not from faith. For by this vocation the will of every predestined person is excited that he may believe efficaciously, even if he is so averse and fierce that he persecutes believers, Augustine, Against Two Letters of the Pelagians, book 1, chapter 19.
pass_b: Sum: there is a special vocation of mercy given to some — not because they were already counted faithful, but because they were predestined to become faithful. It flows from an antecedent will that infallibly destines them to eternal life. Not everyone has that vocation — only the elect. So election hangs on God's good pleasure, not on human act. So it is unto faith, not from faith. By this calling every predestined will is stirred to believe efficaciously — even if so hostile and fierce that he persecutes believers (Augustine, Against Two Letters of the Pelagians 1.19).
